headline_marked: [[Understanding the ruling on Qada prayer]]: Doubts and solutions for missed prayers
headline: Understanding the ruling on Qada prayer: Doubts and solutions for missed prayers
summary: Many Muslims have questions about making up prayers missed due to busyness, forgetfulness, or intentional oversight. Islamic jurisprudence provides clear guidance on the obligation and methods for Qada prayers.
details: In Islam, performing prayers at their prescribed times is obligatory. However, due to daily busy schedules, forgetfulness, or even unintentional mistakes, many individuals miss their regular prayers, leading to questions about 'Qada' (making up) prayers.

Qada prayer refers to fulfilling a missed prayer after its designated time, thereby absolving oneself of the responsibility. The Quran emphasizes performing prayers at specific times, but Islamic Sharia, through clear Hadith and scholarly consensus, confirms the existence and obligation of Qada.

For unintentionally missed prayers, such as those due to sleep or forgetfulness, it is obligatory to perform them as soon as one remembers. Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) himself performed Qada for Asr prayer during the Battle of Khandaq when it was missed due to intense fighting.

Intentionally abandoning prayer without a valid reason is considered a major sin by unanimous consensus across the four major Islamic schools of thought (Madhabs). These schools agree that even in such cases, alongside sincere repentance, it is essential to perform Qada for all previously missed prayers.

A minority of scholars, including Imam Ibn Hazm and Ibn Taymiyyah, held a differing view, arguing that intentionally missed prayers cannot be made up. They cited the time-bound nature of prayer and the absence of direct commands for Qada in such specific scenarios.

However, the majority of jurists (Jumhur Ulama) refuted these views, emphasizing that if Allah's right is not cancelled for unintentional omissions, it certainly isn't for intentional neglect. They also highlighted the principle that "Allah's debt is most deserving of being paid" and drew analogies with the Qada of intentionally broken Ramadan fasts.

The safest course of action, according to the unanimous opinion of the four Madhabs, is to sincerely repent to Allah for past mistakes and make a firm resolve never to miss prayers again. Muslims are advised to estimate the number of prayers missed since adulthood and systematically make them up to fulfill their religious obligations.
caption:

headline_marked: [[Tk 12 crore luxury cars seized]] at Chattogram port, declared as spare parts
headline: Tk 12 crore luxury cars seized at Chattogram port, declared as spare parts
summary: Customs Intelligence seized four luxury cars and components of two others, valued at Tk 12 crore, at Chattogram port. They were allegedly imported from Japan as used motor vehicle spare parts to evade high import duties.
details: The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate has seized four luxury cars and key components of two other vehicles, collectively valued at around Tk 12 crore, at Chattogram port.
The seized vehicles include two Lexus cars, a Honda, and a BMW. Major components for two additional vehicles were also confiscated in the operation.
Customs intelligence officials disclosed these details to journalists at Chattogram port yesterday, highlighting a significant case of alleged import duty evasion.

Dhaka-based Crown Automobile Services imported the consignment from Japan, consisting of 167 packages weighing 8,018 kg. The shipment was declared as used motor vehicle spare parts and used petrol engines, including gearboxes.

The consignment arrived at Chattogram port on July 10, but the importer failed to submit a bill of entry for nearly a month. Customs officials acted on a tip-off that the importer intended to release the goods through auction.

Sagar Sen, joint director of the Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate, stated that the importer appeared to have attempted to clear the vehicles by misdeclaring them as spare parts to pay minimal duties.

Had these vehicles been imported and assessed as complete cars, the government would have been entitled to tariffs ranging from 103 percent to 621 percent of their assessable value, resulting in substantial revenue loss.
Officials are now investigating whether the vehicles were genuinely imported as spare parts or if they were deliberately cut into sections for import and intended for reassembly in Bangladesh.
The financial transactions related to the consignment are also under scrutiny to determine if any money laundering activities were involved in the scheme.
